source_user: Choose between tensor and pipeline parallelism for a latency-sensitive multi-GPU service. State the assumptions needed. Scenario variant 85: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: compare per-GPU memory, communication topology, layer partitioning, batch and microbatch behavior, synchronization, latency target, and failure/reconfiguration costs.
corrected_answer:
Decision framework and assumptions: choose tensor parallelism (TP) when the model must be split within a layer and fast, high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU communication is available; choose pipeline parallelism (PP) when layer-wise partitioning fits each GPU and the topology or memory profile makes frequent intra-layer collectives too costly. Freeze model revision, tokenizer, precision, kernel/runtime versions, GPU count and types, topology, request mix, context/output length distributions, concurrency, SLOs, and fault budget. Do not infer a platform-specific winner without these measurements. Include replicated embeddings/LM head, optimizer or serving buffers, KV-cache placement, and any uneven layer sizes in the memory accounting.

Falsifiable hypothesis: for the stated latency-sensitive workload, the selected scheme meets the p50 and p99 end-to-end latency targets at the required throughput while keeping every GPU below a prespecified memory watermark and correctness threshold. For TP, hypothesize that collective communication time per layer is smaller than the latency and utilization penalty of PP bubbles; for PP, hypothesize that stage transfer plus pipeline bubbles is smaller than TP collective overhead. Falsify the choice if a gate fails, if tail latency or queueing worsens at target concurrency, if stage imbalance/bubbles or collectives dominate, or if failure recovery exceeds the stated budget.

Memory and placement analysis: estimate and then measure per-GPU weights, activations, temporary workspaces, replicated parameters, communication buffers, and KV cache in GiB, including peak rather than only steady state. For TP, document tensor shard dimensions, all-reduce/all-gather/reduce-scatter locations and bytes per token; for PP, document contiguous layer assignment, activation-transfer bytes, stage memory, and the slowest stage. Check divisibility, kernel support, load balance, and whether sequence length or microbatching changes the peak.

Controlled experiment: run the same warmed, checksum-identified service with TP and PP on the same hardware and topology. Use a held-out workload stratified by prompt length, output length, and concurrency; identical decoding and admission policy; randomized or interleaved run order; fixed warmup; and enough repeated trials to report median, p95/p99, confidence intervals, and paired differences. Record request-level TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, queue time, throughput (requests/s and tokens/s), achieved batch/microbatch size, GPU utilization, peak memory, stage idle/bubble time, collective and transfer durations, retries, errors, and quality/correctness results. Verify outputs against a reference with tolerance appropriate to the precision and record dropped, timed-out, or retried requests rather than hiding them.

Confounders and operations: control thermal clocks, placement, background load, network/PCIe/NVLink state, allocator warm-up, batching policy, cache reuse, request ordering, and failed-request treatment. Test single-request and target-concurrency cases separately; PP microbatch count can trade bubbles for memory and latency, while TP communication can saturate links. Exercise a bounded worker/GPU loss or restart separately from the performance trial: define checkpoint/state restoration, in-flight request handling, drain/retry behavior, re-sharding or stage reassignment, expected recovery time, and data-loss limits. Do not claim resilience from a benchmark that did not inject faults.

Rollout: canary the chosen configuration at low traffic with a fixed abort window. Roll back to the last known-good configuration if any latency, error, memory-watermark, correctness, throughput, or recovery gate breaches its prespecified limit; preserve logs and artifacts. If neither scheme meets the SLO, report that result and evaluate fewer replicas, a different GPU/topology, batching, quantization, or a hybrid only as a new controlled experiment. Mark all unmeasured topology, kernel, and fault assumptions as evidence_required.

quality_dimensions.coverage: TP/PP memory, topology, layer partitioning, batching, synchronization, latency, measurement, confounders, failure/reconfiguration, rollback and evidence
quality_dimensions.technical_accuracy: conditional recommendation with explicit assumptions and measured-versus-estimated separation
quality_dimensions.actionability: reproducible paired benchmark and rollout gates

risks: unmeasured topology or kernel support may reverse the recommendation
pipeline imbalance and bubble estimates are workload-dependent
fault recovery is unestablished without injection testing
peak KV-cache and workspace memory can exceed steady-state estimates
evidence_required: hardware interconnect/topology and GPU inventory
model layer shapes, precision, KV-cache policy, and peak memory telemetry
TP collective and PP transfer traces
stratified repeated latency/throughput results with confidence intervals
correctness comparison and bounded failure-injection recovery results

source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: compare per-GPU memory, communication topology, layer partitioning, batch and microbatch behavior, synchronization, latency target, and failure/reconfiguration costs.
corrected_answer:
Decision framework and assumptions: choose tensor parallelism (TP) when the model must be split within a layer and fast, high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU communication is available; choose pipeline parallelism (PP) when layer-wise partitioning fits each GPU and the topology or memory profile makes frequent intra-layer collectives too costly. Freeze model revision, tokenizer, precision, kernel/runtime versions, GPU count and types, topology, request mix, context/output length distributions, concurrency, SLOs, and fault budget. Do not infer a platform-specific winner without these measurements. Include replicated embeddings/LM head, optimizer or serving buffers, KV-cache placement, and any uneven layer sizes in the memory accounting.

Falsifiable hypothesis: for the stated latency-sensitive workload, the selected scheme meets the p50 and p99 end-to-end latency targets at the required throughput while keeping every GPU below a prespecified memory watermark and correctness threshold. For TP, hypothesize that collective communication time per layer is smaller than the latency and utilization penalty of PP bubbles; for PP, hypothesize that stage transfer plus pipeline bubbles is smaller than TP collective overhead. Falsify the choice if a gate fails, if tail latency or queueing worsens at target concurrency, if stage imbalance/bubbles or collectives dominate, or if failure recovery exceeds the stated budget.

Memory and placement analysis: estimate and then measure per-GPU weights, activations, temporary workspaces, replicated parameters, communication buffers, and KV cache in GiB, including peak rather than only steady state. For TP, document tensor shard dimensions, all-reduce/all-gather/reduce-scatter locations and bytes per token; for PP, document contiguous layer assignment, activation-transfer bytes, stage memory, and the slowest stage. Check divisibility, kernel support, load balance, and whether sequence length or microbatching changes the peak.

Controlled experiment: run the same warmed, checksum-identified service with TP and PP on the same hardware and topology. Use a held-out workload stratified by prompt length, output length, and concurrency; identical decoding and admission policy; randomized or interleaved run order; fixed warmup; and enough repeated trials to report median, p95/p99, confidence intervals, and paired differences. Record request-level TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end latency, queue time, throughput (requests/s and tokens/s), achieved batch/microbatch size, GPU utilization, peak memory, stage idle/bubble time, collective and transfer durations, retries, errors, and quality/correctness results. Verify outputs against a reference with tolerance appropriate to the precision and record dropped, timed-out, or retried requests rather than hiding them.

Confounders and operations: control thermal clocks, placement, background load, network/PCIe/NVLink state, allocator warm-up, batching policy, cache reuse, request ordering, and failed-request treatment. Test single-request and target-concurrency cases separately; PP microbatch count can trade bubbles for memory and latency, while TP communication can saturate links. Exercise a bounded worker/GPU loss or restart separately from the performance trial: define checkpoint/state restoration, in-flight request handling, drain/retry behavior, re-sharding or stage reassignment, expected recovery time, and data-loss limits. Do not claim resilience from a benchmark that did not inject faults.

Rollout: canary the chosen configuration at low traffic with a fixed abort window. Roll back to the last known-good configuration if any latency, error, memory-watermark, correctness, throughput, or recovery gate breaches its prespecified limit; preserve logs and artifacts. If neither scheme meets the SLO, report that result and evaluate fewer replicas, a different GPU/topology, batching, quantization, or a hybrid only as a new controlled experiment. Mark all unmeasured topology, kernel, and fault assumptions as evidence_required.
